technique: sound — the consonants and vowels doing quiet work, worth saying aloud
poem:
Woodsmoke sits low in the cold before you move,
the cured-leaf smell of things gone brown and done,
apples somewhere soft in the grass, half-turned,
a sweetness with the rot already in it.
That's fall — it gives and takes in the same breath,
and you've learned not to argue with the trade.
The grey comes up without a word of thanks,
no fanfare, just the hills resolving slow.
Your boots wait by the door where you kicked them off.
There's water to be changed, a root to check,
a handful of small lives that don't ask much —
only that the one who tends them wakes.

So — up!

The kettle's cold, the light's still grey — but the day doesn't start itself, and there's a good hour in it with your name on it.

So — up!
lesson: Today we work on one thing, sound. Sound means the way the consonants and vowels feel in your mouth and ear when you say the words out loud. Listen to cured leaf smell of things gone brown and done. The words gone, brown and done share a low round vowel sound. Say them and you feel your mouth stay open and heavy. Now hear a sweetness with the rot already in it. The soft S and T sounds there move quick and light. This works because repeated sounds make certain words pulled together in your ear. The heavy vowels slow you and make the line feel tired and settled. The quick sounds make a line move faster. You feel the mood for the sound before you even think about the meaning. Try this, pick three words in a row that share one vowel sound and say them aloud to test the weight. The second time through, listen for how so up sounds short and sharp after all the slow, heavy lines before it. Here is the poem.
